Getting started with pitw

Source: vignettes/pitw.Rmd
pitw.Rmd

pitw compares a set of continuous predictive distributions with the values they were meant to predict. For example, given forecasts of a hospital admission rate and the corresponding observed rates, we can check whether the predictive distributions tend to be too narrow or too wide after accounting for a common location bias.

For each observation, the probability integral transform (PIT) gives the proportion of its predictive distribution below the observed value. For calibrated continuous predictions these proportions should be uniform between zero and one. The package summarises departures from uniformity in three ways.

Score Interpretation
B_pit Overall departure from uniformity in the original PIT values. Bias, spread and distribution shape can all contribute.
U_pit Departure that remains after estimating and adjusting for one common location shift.
D_pit Direction of the remaining spread discrepancy. Positive values indicate overconfidence and negative values indicate underconfidence.

Score a set of forecasts

We use 100 reference quantiles of a standard normal distribution as example observations. Each forecast is normal with mean 0.5 and standard deviation 0.7, so the forecasts are displaced and too narrow by construction.

observed <- stats::qnorm(stats::ppoints(100))

pitw::pit_w(true_value = observed, location = 0.5, scale = 0.7)
## # A tibble: 1 × 5
##   B_pit  U_pit  D_pit adjust link    
##   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>  <chr>   
## 1 0.159 0.0556 0.0556 link   identity

The positive D_pit shows that the forecasts are too narrow after adjustment for the common shift. This example illustrates the scores. The significance tests use large-sample reference distributions and assume independent predictions, which matters when forecasts or estimates use overlapping data.

pit_w() scores one set of predictions. Use prediction_scores() to score several sets in a grouped data frame and compare the PIT scores with coverage, interval width and the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS).

Read the vignettes in order

  1. PIT histograms and forecast calibration. Use simulated forecasts to see how location bias and predictive spread change the histogram.
  2. The three PIT-Wasserstein scores. See how the scores are calculated and how they behave alongside coverage and CRPS.
  3. Scoring reproduction number estimates from EpiEstim. Compare five window settings across epidemic sizes, scoring one \(R_t\) estimate per independent series at each setting.
  4. Significance testing. See how to use the reference distributions and which assumptions matter for interpretation.
  5. Sample size and power. Compare how the scores separate known differences as the number of predictions increases.
  6. Predictive distribution shape. See what happens when forecasts use a different distributional family, including cases where width and tail differences produce similar scores.
